GAUTENG SCHOOL PLACEMENTS

By: Ntokozo Miya | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Meant to make school placement convenient and give learners access to schools that they previously could not attend, some parents say the Gauteng online system has failed them and their children.

Unique Selling Point:
We track the progress of the controversial Gauteng online school placement system from the perspective of parents.

Summary:
Launched in May 2019 for the 2020 school year by the Gauteng Education MEC Panyaza Lesufi, the online system for school placements was meant to allow pupils to attend schools in areas that were previously inaccessible by increasing the feeder radius from a historic 5km distance to 30km.

This came after the Constitutional Court ruled in favour of Lesufi's bid to address apartheid spatial planning by expanding the radius in 2016. The department then took the time that followed to determine the feeding zones and eventually launched the online system in May 2019.

Some parents complain that they have been placed at schools they did not prefer while others have received no placement offers at all. On the other hand, the department says thousands of parents have not accepted the placement offers. We also speak to key sector players including education specialists and organisations opposed to the system. In fact, on Tuesday, AfriForum launched its petition to remove Panyaza Lesufi as the Gauteng MEC for Education mainly due to Lesufi's handling of the registration process which is reported to have left 14 000 grade 1 and 8 pupils without school placement. What does this mean for unplaced scholars in the coming year? What adjustments will parents and scholars have to make in reaction to being accepted at schools that they did not plan for?

Further information:
The criteria for school placement is as follows, in order of priority:

1. Area where you live

2. Learners who have a sibling at a school

3. If the place of employment of any of the parents is within the feeder zone of the school

4. If learner's place of residence is within a 30km radius of the school

5. If the learner wants to be placed in a school of focussed learning

6. If the applicant learner's place of residence is beyond the 30km radius of the school

Script:


GAUTENG SCHOOL PLACEMENTS

VIDEO / NOTES
AUDIO


VO – Parents want to give their children the best start in life...for that, quality education is key.
But in Gauteng, some parents worry that they will be unable to do that.
Carin Rossouw from Olifantsfontein, South of Pretoria has a daughter Kayla in Grade 9 at a local high school and a son Kian, who will be in Grade 8 next year.
She applied for Kian at the same school as his sister.


CARIN ROSSOUW - PARENT
It is the closest public Afrikaans speaking school to where we live.


VO – Earlier this year, the Gauteng education department expanded the online placement process, allowing parents for the first time to apply for schools within thirty kilometers of their homes as opposed to the limited five kilometer radius of the past.
The NGO Equal Education does extensive research in the education sector, and researcher Rone McFarlane says the radius extension gives learners access to schools they could not attend before.


RONÉ MCFARLANE – EQUAL EDUCATION
The idea is that we move beyond the apartheid spatial planning which meant that wealthy suburbs are generally around well-performing schools.


VO – Parents can apply to as many as five schools. Ideally, once the electronic application is processed, the learner is placed at one of their choices. Carin only applied to one school.


CARIN ROSSOUW - PARENT
The only response I received was that the school is potentially full. The school that we have been placed in is much further away.


VO - While some parents are thrilled with the radius extension, many want a school closer to home.


LINK – The scramble for the best schools in Gauteng is in full force and some parents say the online system that should have made school applications simple and fair, has in fact, worked against them.


VO – Many parents who cannot afford private or independent schools, rely on public schools.
To place Grade 1 and Grade 8 learners, the system examines a number of criteria.


UPSOUND – EDUCATION DEPT. TUTORIAL VIDEO
Preference will be given to learners who live closest to the school within the feeder zone. Second, learners who have a brother or sister in the school you want to apply to.


VO – Despite meeting the top two criteria for placement, Carin still couldn’t secure a place for her son at the nearby school.


CARIN ROSSOUW – PARENT
He is unhappy that he may potentially not go to a school that he would like to go.


VO – But some parents, like Wanda Qobo of Boksburg east of Joburg, say the system favoured them.
Wanda has a daughter Lelo, who starts Grade 1 next year and another, Noma who will be in Grade 8.
Noma’s application went through smoothly.


WANDA QONDO – PARENT
I did the application at 3 different schools. I chose those schools because they are good schools in the area and in pretty close proximity. She got accepted at two of the schools and then we get to pick one.


VO – The new system was the brainchild of Gauteng’s Education MEC Panyaza Lesufi – his motivation, to improve access to good schools for learners across the board.


RONÉ MCFARLANE – EQUAL EDUCATION
Lesufi tweeted that parents must please take note that the majority of our good schools are full – what it essentially means is that they are saying to parents that there is no space for your child in a good school.


VO – These ten top schools reached full capacity within 24 hours of the system going live. They are all located in affluent suburbs.
Wanda is satisfied with Noma's placement but can't say the same about the outcome for young Lelo.


WANDA QOBO – PARENT
You take into mind the type of school it is, the school culture that they have – things like the academics, if they sport activities. I wouldn't have picked that school.


LINK – While some parents fear that they might indeed end up having to brave this much traffic transporting their kids to distant schools, others are worried they might not even find a school for their children.


VO – As of late this week, of the three hundred and ten thousand, three hundred and fifty applications that the department received, the Department said fewer than nine thousand learners had yet to be placed.
The department has built over forty new schools and renovated many others...but quality education is about more than nice buildings.


RONÉ MCFARLANE – EQUAL EDUCATION
The way in which schools are set up and the resources they have access to allow them to protect teaching and learning is fundamental to contributing to quality education. That's about the types of learners those schools admit, the resources that those learners bring with them including prior learning, the fees that school is able to charge, the number of teachers that it's able to employ.


VO – Lesufi’s spokesperson Steve Mabona says the online applications have exposed certain schools for poor performance.


STEVE MABONA – GAUTENG EDUCATION DEPARTMENT
DEREK – Putting it bluntly, are some of the schools that have received the least applications in the townships?
MABONA – Indeed. The focal point was to invest more in the township schools. Our educators are being trained. We gave them laptops, we gave our learners tablets.


VO – Despite parents being assigned schools that are far away, Mabona says there is no problem with the system.


STEVE MABONA – GAUTENG EDUCATION DEPARTMENT
When you go to school and submit the documents, then the officials must verify and check against the application to say parent X has applied and in the system there is an address and physically these are the documents that we see so where would a system error be there, in terms of the addresses?
DEREK – Many parents got offers from distant schools, although they found out that there were spaces at their preferred school nearby...
MABONA – There are schools that will be silly...to say: “We have space, don't worry, we should be in a position to accommodate you...
DEREK – So they are not telling the truth at the schools?
MABONA – There are schools that are lying.


VO – But as Mabona takes us down to the Department’s service centre, several angry parents take their chance to demand answers.


MMAPITSO MOREWA – PARENT
My son, he's got siblings in that school and the address is within that area, but he has not been accepted and I want to know from the department: “What's going on?”
DEREK - But we are told that they are doing everything to accommodate you and your learners?
MAPULA MOTABE – PARENT
You must wait for 21 days and they will attend you after 21 days? Why must we get such responses if they are doing everything to help us?


LINK - Well, many angry parents. I think Steve is trying to help them but the temperature is rising.


LUCILLE GOUWS – PARENT
I am the parent. I know why I chose that school so no one else is going to tell me: “Send your child to that school.” No, no!



LINK – The department insists every learner will be assigned a school but parents fear that their children will end up at the very schools they were trying to avoid.


VO – The Department expects more applications from parents who did not apply at all this year.



STEVE MABONA – GAUTENG EDUCATION DEPARTMENT
We anticipate that we might even get about 18 000 of those.
DEREK – You've got, let's be honest, more than 25 000 families who are traumatised, worrying about the future for their children?
MABONA – We'll never get tired to apologise to all our parents. We are just hoping that they will understand that capacity is our challenge.

PROMOS
In Gauteng, many parents are fuming. They say the online school placement system has put their children at the distant, under-performing schools they were trying to avoid.
It’s year-end and at this late stage, some Gauteng parents still don’t know if their kids will find a good school for next year, they say the online placement system has failed them.
What was meant to be a simple and fair online school placement system has failed some Gauteng learners – leaving them far from where they wanted to be and uncertain about the future.
